title: 60 SQL Practice Queries with Answers (PostgreSQL)
summary: Sixty PostgreSQL practice queries on an employees/departments/orders schema. They run from basic SELECT and filtering through aggregates, joins, subqueries, window functions and CTEs to classic interview scenarios, and each comes with its solution and result.

chapters.title: Basics: SELECT, Aliases and Sorting
points: List all columns for every row in employees
Select only the name and salary columns from employees
Rename salary to monthly_pay with a column alias
Compute annual salary as salary * 12 in the SELECT list
Sort employees by salary from highest to lowest
Return the 5 highest-paid employees with ORDER BY and LIMIT

chapters.title: Filtering with WHERE
points: Find employees in department 10 with an equality filter
Find employees earning between 50000 and 80000 using BETWEEN
Find employees in departments 10, 20 or 30 using IN
Find employees whose name starts with 'A' using LIKE
Find employees with no manager using IS NULL
Find orders from 2024 that are not cancelled, combining AND, OR and NOT with correct parentheses
Return the distinct set of job titles with DISTINCT
Page through employees by skipping the first 10 rows with OFFSET

chapters.title: Aggregates, GROUP BY and HAVING
points: Count the total number of employees
Find the average salary across the company
Find the highest and lowest salary in one query
Count employees per department with GROUP BY
Find the total order amount per customer
List departments with more than 5 employees using HAVING
Find the average salary per job title, rounded to 2 decimals
Count how many employees have a NULL manager versus how many do not, using COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)

chapters.title: Joins
points: List each employee with their department name using INNER JOIN
List all departments including those with no employees using LEFT JOIN
Find departments that have no employees with LEFT JOIN and IS NULL
Find employees who earn more than their manager using a self join
List each employee next to their manager's name
Find customers who have never placed an order with an anti-join
Show total order amount per department by joining three tables
Generate every employee and project-role pairing with CROSS JOIN

chapters.title: Subqueries
points: Find employees earning more than the company average salary with a scalar subquery
Find employees who work in the department with the highest headcount
Find employees whose department is in the list of departments located in 'Mumbai' using IN with a subquery
Find customers who have placed at least one order using EXISTS
Find customers who have never ordered using NOT EXISTS
Find employees earning more than the average of their own department with a correlated subquery

chapters.title: Window Functions
points: Number every employee by salary with ROW_NUMBER()
Rank employees by salary with ties using RANK()
Rank employees by salary without gaps using DENSE_RANK()
Rank employees by salary within each department with PARTITION BY
Show each employee's salary next to the department average using AVG() OVER
Show each order beside the previous order's amount for the same customer using LAG()

chapters.title: CTEs
points: Rewrite an average-salary subquery as a WITH clause
Chain two CTEs: department totals, then departments above the overall average
Find the top earner in each department with a CTE and ROW_NUMBER()
Walk the full management chain for one employee using WITH RECURSIVE
Generate the numbers 1 to 10 with a recursive CTE
Delete duplicate rows using a CTE with DELETE ... RETURNING

chapters.title: Interview Scenarios I: Ranking and Duplicates
points: Find the second highest salary using LIMIT and OFFSET
Find the nth highest salary (n = 3) using DENSE_RANK()
Find the second highest salary in each department
Find duplicate emails with GROUP BY and HAVING
Return only the duplicate rows beyond the first using ROW_NUMBER()
Find employees who share the same salary as another employee

chapters.title: Interview Scenarios II: Running Totals and Trends
points: Compute a running total of order amount by date with SUM() OVER (ORDER BY ...)
Compute a 3-row moving average of daily sales with ROWS BETWEEN
Compute month-over-month sales growth with LAG()
Find the top 3 customers by spend in each month
Find customers who ordered in three consecutive months
Find gaps in a sequence of order ids

chapters.title: Cheatsheet: Picking the Right Query Pattern
points: Find the highest-paid employee: pick MAX(), ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 or a window function
Find rows with no match: pick NOT EXISTS, LEFT JOIN with IS NULL, or NOT IN, and know the NULL trap
Find the top N per group: use ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...) in a CTE
Count conditionally in one pass using COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ...)
Get one row per group with DISTINCT ON in PostgreSQL
Pivot status counts into columns with conditional aggregation
